568.title: Their affairs by consultation
568.hook: the believers conduct their affairs by consultation (42:38)
568.howItsDone: Muslims treat shura, mutual consultation, as a value for families, communities and leadership; scholars have long debated how binding it is on leaders and what forms it should take.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing like Him, and your line was nothing like him. Did the pairs around you, shoes, hands, days, remind you of the One with none? Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Hudaybiya, near Mecca. The Prophet ﷺ has just signed a treaty that many of his companions think is a humiliation. He tells them: get up, sacrifice your animals, and shave your heads. The pilgrimage is over for this year. Nobody moves. He says it three times. Still nobody. He goes into his tent, to his wife Umm Salama, and tells her what's happened. And she gives him advice that changes the afternoon. Bukhari records it. We'll come back to what she said. First, the verse that gives this surah its name.

Surah Ash-Shura, verse thirty-eight, part of a list describing the believers. Pickthall: "And those who answer the call of their Lord and establish worship, and whose affairs are a matter of counsel, and who spend of what We have bestowed on them." Look at the company consultation keeps. Prayer on one side. Giving on the other. Shura, consultation, sits right between two of the pillars, as part of the description of a believer, not as a management tip. And here's a detail: this surah is from Mecca, before there was any Muslim state, any government, any council. Consultation was described as a habit of believers before there was anything to govern. Back on day three hundred seventy-three, we heard the Prophet told to consult his companions, even after a consultation went badly. Today, the believers are described as doing it with each other. And now, back to the tent at Hudaybiya. Umm Salama said: Messenger of Allah, do you want them to do it? Then go out, don't say a word to anyone, and sacrifice your animal, and call your barber to shave your head. He did exactly that. And when the companions saw him do it, they got up, sacrificed, and began shaving each other's heads, so eagerly, the report says, that they almost hurt each other. A prophet, receiving revelation, asked his wife what to do, and took her advice. Many scholars point to this as a model: consultation isn't a formality, and good counsel can come from the person you least expect.

The practice: decide something together. Sit, and think of one decision coming up, small or large: dinner, a trip, a change at work, how to spend a weekend. Who else does it touch? Picture asking them, really asking, before you've decided. What might they see that you don't? Choose one person, and plan when you'll ask today. Then rest, without carrying the decision alone. The bell holds the time.
Their affairs by consultation. Ash-Shura thirty-eight: the believers settle their affairs by counsel among themselves, between prayer and giving. Today's word.
Your line: consult. Today, before you decide one thing that touches someone else, ask them first, and listen to the answer. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

569.title: Daughters and sons
569.hook: He gives daughters to whom He wills, sons, or both, or none (42:49–50)
569.howItsDone: Muslims greet the birth of a child with thanks to Allah and often an 'aqiqah celebration for both girls and boys; the hadith on raising daughters is widely taught as an honor for parents of girls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, their affairs by consultation, and your line was consult. Did you ask someone before deciding something that touched them? Day five hundred sixty-nine.

In seventh-century Arabia, the Qur'an describes a scene it clearly wants to end. A man is told his wife has given birth to a girl. His face darkens. He hides from people, ashamed of the news, wondering whether to keep her or bury her in the dust. Surah An-Nahl paints it; Surah At-Takwir says the buried girl will one day be asked for what sin she was killed. Against that background, listen to the order of the words in Surah Ash-Shura, when it talks about children. Who gets named first.

Verse forty-nine. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Pickthall: "He createth what He will." Then: He gives daughters to whomever He wills, and sons to whomever He wills. Daughters first. In a culture where a daughter's birth could darken a father's face, the Qur'an lists girls ahead of boys, as gifts. Some early scholars noticed this; one is reported to have said that it's a blessing for a woman when her first child is a girl, because Allah began with daughters. Verse fifty continues: or He gives both, sons and daughters, and He makes whom He wills childless. He is Knowing, Able. Four possibilities: daughters, sons, both, or none. Every one of them is placed in Allah's hands. Which means none of them is a verdict on the parents. Not a reward for having sons. Not a punishment for having daughters, or no children at all. The Qur'an's own stories show it. Ibrahim and Zakariyya waited into old age. 'A'isha, the Prophet's wife, had no children, and she became one of the most important teachers in early Islam. The Prophet ﷺ himself had sons who died young, and it was through his daughter Fatima that his family continued. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim gives raising girls a special honor: whoever raises two daughters until they're grown, the Prophet said, will come on the Day of Resurrection with me like this, and he held two fingers together. The verse lists four gifts, and the hadith makes sure the first one is never treated as the lesser.

The practice: thank Allah for the children around you. Sit, and bring them to mind one by one: your own, if you have them, or nieces and nephews, neighbors' kids, students, a friend's baby, the child you once were. Picture each face for a breath. If you pray, thank Allah for each one. If not, simply be grateful. And if there's an ache here, a child hoped for or lost, let it be part of the sitting too. The bell holds the time.
Daughters and sons. Ash-Shura forty-nine and fifty: Allah gives daughters, sons, both, or none, and daughters are named first. Today's word.
Your line: each gift is his. Today, say something kind to or about a girl in your life, a daughter, a niece, a student, and let her hear that she's a gift. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

570.title: Silver roofs
570.hook: if not for people all becoming one in disbelief, the deniers would have had silver roofs, and it's all the enjoyment of this life (43:33–35)
570.howItsDone: Muslim teaching on zuhd, detachment from worldly things, often cites Az-Zukhruf 33–35 and the Prophet's simple room; many Muslims understand wealth as a trust to be used well, not a sign of God's favor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daughters and sons, and your line was each gift is his. Did a girl in your life hear that she's a gift? Today, a new surah, Az-Zukhruf, the Ornaments. Day five hundred seventy.

'Umar walks into a small room in Medina and finds the Prophet ﷺ lying on a rough mat of palm fiber, with nothing between it and his skin. When he sits up, the weave has left lines pressed into his side. A leather pillow stuffed with fiber. A little barley in the corner. 'Umar looks around and starts to cry. He's thinking of the kings of Persia and Rome, in their palaces, and here is the Messenger of Allah on a mat. The Prophet asks him why he's crying. His answer, in Bukhari, is close to today's verses.

Surah Az-Zukhruf, verses thirty-three to thirty-five. The surah is pushing back on a claim it quotes a few verses earlier: if this message were true, wouldn't it have come to some great man of the two cities, someone rich? So the Qur'an answers with an image. If it weren't that all people would become one community of deniers, chasing it, Allah would have given those who deny the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and silver stairways to climb, and doors, and couches to lean on, and zukhruf, gold ornament. Then the verdict: all of that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world, and the hereafter with your Lord is for the mindful. The argument is striking. Silver roofs are so cheap, in Allah's eyes, that He'd hand them out to people who reject Him, except that everyone would then follow the silver. Wealth isn't a sign of being favored. It's not even the scale anything is weighed on. Zukhruf, the surah's name, means gilding: gold leaf on the surface. Beautiful, and thin. Back to 'Umar in the little room. The Prophet answered him: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the hereafter? Not a rule against owning things; the companions included merchants and the wealthy. A rule about where the weight goes. And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says it even more sharply: if this world were worth a mosquito's wing to Allah, He wouldn't give a denier a sip of water from it.
screen: `THEY HAVE THIS WORLD; WE, THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice an ornament you want. Sit, and let something come to mind that you've wanted lately: a phone, a kitchen, a car, a look, a kind of house. Don't judge the wanting. Just see it clearly. Now picture it a few years from now: scratched, out of date, replaced. Notice which part of you still wants it after that. Then let it rest, lightly, like gold leaf. The bell holds the time.
Silver roofs. Az-Zukhruf's picture: silver roofs and gold ornament, so cheap to Allah He'd give them to deniers, all only the enjoyment of this life. Today's word.
Your line: ornaments pass. Today, when you catch yourself wanting something shiny, ask: will this still matter when the gilding wears off? Day five hundred seventy.

571.title: Friends that day
571.hook: friends that day will be enemies, except the mindful (43:67)
571.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to choose companions who help them toward good, and the hadith of the perfume seller and the blacksmith is often taught to young people about friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, silver roofs, and your line was ornaments pass. Did you catch yourself wanting something shiny, and ask if it would last? Day five hundred seventy-one.

Picture two kinds of shops on a market street. One sells perfume. Walk in, and even if you buy nothing, you leave smelling good, or at least you've breathed something lovely for a few minutes. Next door is a blacksmith, working the bellows. Walk in there, and if a spark doesn't burn your clothes, you'll leave smelling of smoke. The Prophet ﷺ used exactly this picture, recorded in both Bukhari and Muslim, to describe friends. Surah Az-Zukhruf takes the same question, who your friends are, and follows it all the way to the Day.

Surah Az-Zukhruf, verse sixty-seven. Pickthall: "Friends on that day will be foes one to another, save those who kept their duty (to Allah)." The Arabic word for friends is al-akhilla', the plural of khalil. Not an acquaintance. A khalil is the closest kind of friend, the one whose love runs through you. Ibrahim is called Khalil Allah, the intimate friend of God. So the verse is talking about the deepest friendships people have. And it says that on the Day, many of them will turn into enmity. Why? Commentators explain: friendships built on doing wrong together, on vanity, on using each other, fall apart when everyone sees what they led to. Each friend blames the other. Another surah gives the voice of such a person: if only I hadn't taken so-and-so as a close friend. But then the exception: except the muttaqin, the mindful, those who kept their duty. Friendships built on goodness don't break that day. They're the ones that last. And the next verse turns straight to them: O My servants, no fear on you today, and you won't grieve. We heard words close to these a few days ago in Fussilat, spoken by angels to those who stand firm. The perfume seller and the blacksmith come back here. A hadith in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi says a person follows the way of their close friend, so let each of you look at whom you befriend. And when a man asked the Prophet about someone who loves a group but can't match their deeds, he answered, in Bukhari: a person will be with those they love. Choose your perfume sellers well.

The practice: spend time with a good friend. Sit, and bring to mind your closest friends. For each one, ask gently: when I leave time with them, do I smell of perfume or smoke? Am I kinder, more honest, more patient? Don't judge anyone. Just notice. Then choose one friend who leaves you better, and plan a call, a walk or a meal with them this week. If you pray, ask that your friendships last beyond this life. The bell holds the time.
Friends that day. Az-Zukhruf sixty-seven: on the Day, close friends become enemies, except the mindful, whose friendship in goodness lasts. Today's word.
Your line: friends in goodness last. Today, reach out to one friend who makes you better, and tell them so. Day five hundred seventy-one.

572.title: A blessed night
572.hook: We sent it down on a blessed night (44:3)
572.howItsDone: Many Muslims spend the odd nights of the last ten days of Ramadan in extra prayer and Qur'an reading, seeking Laylat al-Qadr; some also keep the middle night of Sha'ban, and many pray a short night prayer before dawn year round.

segments.voice: Yesterday, friends that day: the verse that says close friends turn into enemies on the last day, except the mindful. Your line was friends in goodness last. Did you get time with one of them? Day five hundred seventy-two.

Most books don't say when they were written. The Qur'an says it twice, and both times it names not a year or a season but a night. Today we open Surah Ad-Dukhan, the Smoke, the forty-fourth surah. It begins with two Arabic letters, Ha and Mim, that nobody can fully explain, then an oath by the book itself, and then, in the third verse, a time stamp. Not a date. A quality. The night it came down was blessed.

Pickthall's translation of the opening: "Ha. Mim. By the Scripture that maketh plain. Lo! We revealed it on a blessed night." The Arabic for blessed night is laylatin mubarakah. Mubarak comes from baraka, a word you may know from a greeting card: Eid Mubarak. Baraka is blessing that stays and grows, the way a little food somehow feeds a whole table. So which night is it? Most commentators say it is the same night named in Surah Al-Qadr, the ninety-seventh surah: Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, in the last ten nights of Ramadan. Surah Al-Baqarah also says the Qur'an was revealed in the month of Ramadan, and putting those verses together, that reading became the common one. A minority of early voices connected this verse to the middle night of Sha'ban instead, and some Muslims still keep that night with prayer, but the major commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, held to Ramadan. The verse right after says that on this night every wise matter is made distinct, which is why many people pray that night as if the coming year is being written. Then there's the timing itself. Why a night at all? The Qur'an keeps coming back to the dark hours: rising for prayer while others sleep, verses that speak of the night as a covering. A night is when the noise stops. The sources don't explain why this book arrived after sunset rather than at noon, and it's honest to say so. But the people who keep the Night of Power answer with their feet: they stay awake, they pray, they read, waiting for a night that is better than a thousand months.
screen: `HA. MIM. AN OATH BY THE BOOK.` · `MUBARAK: BLESSING THAT STAYS AND GROWS.` · `MOST SAY: THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · `THE QUR'AN LOVES THE NIGHT HOURS.`

segments.voice: The outline's practice is one minute of prayer in the night. You may be hearing this at noon, so start with the minute you have. Sit, and let the room go quiet. Picture the last real dark you remember: a sleeping house, one lamp, nobody needing you. Breathe there. If you pray, you can choose a minute tonight, after everyone is asleep, to pray or to say alhamdulillah slowly. If you don't, set an alarm for one minute of stillness before bed. The bell holds the time.
A blessed night. Laylatin mubarakah: the night the Qur'an came down, which most commentators identify with the Night of Power in Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: a blessed night. Tonight, before you sleep, take one minute in the dark with no screen, and notice what the quiet sounds like. Day five hundred seventy-two.

573.title: The smoke
573.hook: watch for the day the sky brings a visible smoke (44:10)
573.howItsDone: Muslims read Ad-Dukhan as part of the Qur'an's warnings, and many recite it on Thursday nights or Fridays; commentators teach both readings of the smoke, the famine in Mecca and a sign before the Last Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a blessed night, the night the Qur'an came down. Did you find your minute in the dark, and what did the quiet sound like? Day five hundred seventy-three.

Hunger does strange things to the eyes. People who have gone long without food describe the world going gray at the edges, as if a haze has settled over everything. Hold that picture. The surah we opened yesterday takes its name from one word in its tenth verse: dukhan, smoke. And the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ did not agree about what that smoke was. One of them thought it had already happened, in a hungry year in Mecca. Others thought it was still coming.

Here is the verse in Pickthall's translation: "But watch thou for the day when the sky will produce visible smoke." The next verse says it will cover the people, a painful torment, and the people cry out to their Lord to remove it. Then the surah says it will be lifted for a little while, and they will return to their ways. Two readings come down from the earliest generation. The first is from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. He said the Quraysh of Mecca resisted the Prophet so hard that he prayed against them, and a famine came, years of it, until people ate bones and carrion. A man would look up at the sky and see something like smoke between himself and it, from the hunger. Then the Meccans asked for relief, it came, and they went back to what they had been doing, just as the verses describe. For Ibn Mas'ud, the smoke was a past event. The second reading, linked to 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, says the smoke is one of the great signs before the Last Day. A hadith in Sahih Muslim lists ten signs before the Hour, and the smoke is among them. Many scholars hold both: a smoke that came, and a smoke still to come. What stays the same in every reading is the shape. Something in the sky makes people afraid. They cry out. Relief comes. And then, very quickly, they forget they ever asked. The surah isn't only describing a catastrophe. It's describing how short human memory can be once the air clears.
screen: `WATCH FOR THE VISIBLE SMOKE.` · `IBN MAS'UD: A FAMINE IN MECCA.` · `OTHERS: A SIGN BEFORE THE HOUR.` · `THEY ASK, IT LIFTS, THEY FORGET.`

segments.voice: The practice is simple: notice the air you breathe. Sit, and breathe in through the nose. Feel how cool it is on the way in, how warm on the way out. You didn't earn this air. You didn't ask for it this morning. Think of a day the air was bad: smoke from a fire, a stuffy room, a cold that blocked everything. Then come back to this breath, clear. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for the air itself. The bell holds the time.
The smoke. Dukhan: the sign in 44:10, read by Ibn Mas'ud as a famine haze in Mecca, and by others as a sign still to come. Today's word.
Your line: a sign in the sky. Today, look up once, at clear sky or gray, and remember one time relief came and you forgot to say thank you. Day five hundred seventy-three.

574.title: Desire as a god
574.hook: have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god (45:23)
574.howItsDone: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs and its hawa; many practice small refusals through voluntary fasts on Mondays and Thursdays, and classical spiritual writing treats taming desire as daily work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the smoke, and your line was a sign in the sky. Did you look up, and remember a relief you forgot to give thanks for? Day five hundred seventy-four, the end of the week.

It's eleven at night. You said you'd sleep early. One more episode. Then one more scroll. Then the fridge, for nothing in particular. Nobody forced any of it. Nobody would call it worship, either. It's just wanting, doing what wanting does when nobody stops it. But Surah Al-Jathiyah, the Kneeling, the forty-fifth surah, uses exactly that word. It asks about a person whose wanting has quietly taken the top place in their life, the place where only God belongs.

Pickthall's translation of verse twenty-three begins: "Hast thou seen him who maketh his desire his god." The Arabic word for desire is hawa. Its root carries the sense of falling, or being blown, the way something drops through the air with nothing under it. Hawa is wanting that pulls you along without asking where it's going. The verse doesn't say desire is evil. Islam has room for appetite: food, marriage, rest, beauty, all of these are blessed in their place. The problem the verse names is rank. When the wanting decides and everything else obeys, the wanting has become a god, even if the person never bowed to an idol in their life. The rest of the verse is sobering: it speaks of hearing and heart sealed, and a covering on the sight. The scholars read that as what slowly happens when every choice runs one way. Classical writers turned this into a whole teaching. Al-Ghazali, the eleventh-century scholar, wrote at length about the struggle with the nafs, the self that wants, and he compared it to a horse: strong, useful, and only safe when it has a rider. Another verse in the Qur'an, in Surah An-Nazi'at, praises the one who feared standing before his Lord and held the self back from hawa. So the word is not a word for sin. It's a word for direction. Is the horse carrying you, or are you being carried off? This week has moved through consultation, daughters and sons, silver roofs, friends that last, a blessed night and a smoke in the sky. It ends on the oldest question: who, or what, sits on the throne inside you.
screen: `HAWA: DESIRE THAT PULLS YOU ALONG.` · `NOT EVIL, BUT OUT OF RANK.` · `THE SELF AS A HORSE NEEDING A RIDER.` · `WHO SITS ON THE THRONE INSIDE?`

segments.voice: The outline's practice: refuse one craving. Sit, and breathe. Let one small craving come up: a snack, your phone, a purchase, a reply you want to send too fast. Don't fight it. Just watch it, the way you'd watch weather. Notice where it lives in the body. Then decide, quietly, that this one will wait until tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask for help holding it. The bell holds the time.
Hawa. Desire that pulls you along, the wanting that 45:23 warns can take a god's place when nothing else is allowed to rank above it. Today's word.
Your line: not my desire's servant. Today, the first time you reach for something out of pure habit, pause for three seconds and ask who's deciding. Day five hundred seventy-four.

match.prompt: desire as a god — tap the pairs.
pairs: strong, safe only with a rider

myth: the verse says every desire is sinful
it warns about desire taking the top rank, not about appetite itself.
a person can make desire a god without ever bowing to an idol
that is the point of 45:23: rank, not statues.
al-Ghazali wrote about struggling with the nafs
he treated taming the wanting self at length.

fork.setup: you notice a craving at eleven at night. what does 45:23 ask you to look at?
options: who or what is ranking first in your choices.
fork.reveal: the verse is about rank: desire made a god, deciding while everything else obeys.

original.note: Arabic: desire, inclination; the root carries a sense of falling or being blown.

trapdoor: what you thought: wanting things is the problem.
what it means: desire becomes a god when it takes the top place and everything else obeys it.
what a scholar hears: hawa shares a root with falling through the air; 79:40 praises the one who held the self back from hawa.

sources.ref: Qur'an 79:40–41 (holding the self back from desire)
al-Ghazali, Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din, Book of Disciplining the Soul
